D1.1.1.q: A hospital's files are suddenly locked and a message demands payment in Bitcoin to unlock them. What kind of threat is this?
D1.1.1.why: Ransomware is malware that encrypts data and demands payment to release it.

D1.1.2.q: An attacker exploits an unpatched web server to get into a shop's network and download customer records. Which threat is this?
D1.1.2.why: Hacking is gaining access to a system without permission, often through unpatched weaknesses.

D1.1.3.q: A technician spills coffee over a server, which stops working and loses a day's orders. Which threat is this?
D1.1.3.why: Accidental damage is unintentional harm from human error or physical accidents.

D1.1.4.q: Staff get an email that looks like it's from the IT department asking them to click a link and 'confirm' their password. What attack is this?
D1.1.4.why: Social engineering tricks people, not systems, into giving away information or access.

D1.1.5.q: A river floods a company's ground-floor server room, destroying all its on-site storage. What should the company have had to survive this?
D1.1.5.why: Natural disasters destroy hardware on site, so only a copy kept somewhere else lets you recover.

D1.2.1.q: An employee visits a film piracy site on a work PC, and malware is silently installed. Which internal threat is this?
D1.2.1.why: Visiting malicious or banned sites on work systems can bring malware in.

D1.2.2.q: A receptionist emails a spreadsheet of patient details to the wrong person by mistake. What is this?
D1.2.2.why: Sharing data by mistake still counts as a data breach.

D1.2.3.q: On his last day, a salesperson copies the whole customer database onto a USB stick to take to a rival. Which threat is this?
D1.2.3.why: It is a deliberate insider act of copying confidential data to share or sell.

D1.2.4.q: A nurse leaves an unencrypted USB stick of patient records on a train. Which internal threat does this show?
D1.2.4.why: USB sticks, laptops and phones can be lost or bring in malware.

D1.3.1.q: Ransomware encrypts a small firm's only copy of its accounts, and there is no backup. What is the most direct impact?
options: Loss of customers due to public image
D1.3.1.why: With no backup, the data is permanently lost or inaccessible.

D1.3.2.q: After failing to secure customer data, a company is fined by the ICO and sued by affected customers. What impact is this?
options: Financial loss due to legal action
Loss of customers due to public image
D1.3.2.why: ICO fines and lawsuits are financial losses caused by legal action.

D1.3.3.q: After a card data breach makes the news, shoppers stop trusting a retailer and buy from its rivals. Which impact is this?
options: Loss of customers due to public image
Financial loss due to legal action
D1.3.3.why: A public breach damages trust and reputation, so customers leave.

D2.1.1.q: Everyone in a company can open the payroll spreadsheet, but only HR should be able to edit it. What should be set on the file?
options: File permissions (read-only for everyone except HR)
D2.1.1.why: File permissions control who can read, write, run or delete a file.

D2.1.2.q: Staff should see only their own department's systems, while IT admins can manage everything. Which protection is this?
D2.1.2.why: Access levels give each user only the privileges their role needs.

D2.1.3.q: A school copies its data every night to a separate location so it can restore files after a disaster. Which protection is this?
D2.1.3.why: Backups are copies kept elsewhere that can be restored after data loss.

D2.1.4.q: An attacker has stolen a member of staff's password but still can't log in because a code is needed from the staff member's phone. What stopped them?
D2.1.4.why: MFA adds a second factor, so a password alone is not enough.

D2.1.5.q: A lab wants entry that can't be passed on like a swipe card or password, so it scans each person's fingerprint. Which protection is this?
D2.1.5.why: Biometrics use unique body features, which can't easily be shared or forgotten.

D2.1.6.q: A company puts its server room behind a locked door with swipe-card entry and CCTV. Which kind of protection is this?
D2.1.6.why: Physical measures stop unauthorised people reaching IT equipment.

D2.1.7.q: A customer checks the padlock on a bank's website to be sure it is the genuine bank. What issued by a Certificate Authority proves this?
D2.1.7.why: Digital certificates prove a website is genuine and enable encryption.

D2.2.q: A downloaded file matches a known trojan's signature and is moved somewhere it can't run. Which software did this, and what action did it take?
D2.2.why: Antivirus finds malware using signatures and behaviour checks, then quarantines or removes it.

D2.3.q: A business wants to block all incoming network traffic on ports it does not use. What should it configure?
D2.3.why: A firewall monitors traffic in and out and blocks it according to rules.

D2.4.1.q: A sales rep's laptop is stolen, but the thief cannot read any of the files on the drive because BitLocker is turned on. What protected the data?
D2.4.1.why: Encrypting stored data means a stolen device or drive can't be read.

D2.4.2.q: Messages are intercepted on public Wi-Fi as they travel, but the attacker sees only scrambled data. What protected them?
D2.4.2.why: Encrypting data as it travels means it can't be read if it is intercepted.

D2.4.3.q: An online shop's checkout page must encrypt card details between the browser and server and prove the site is genuine. What should it use?
D2.4.3.why: HTTPS is HTTP secured with TLS: it encrypts the traffic and proves the server is genuine.
